name: Sovereignty
scope: The political doctrine of sovereignty as the defining sources state it: supreme authority within a territory, held by a monarch, a legislature, a constitution or the people, whose content the encyclopedias trace through Bodin's and Hobbes's absolute, indivisible sovereignty, Rousseau's and Locke's popular sovereignty, Austin's legislative sovereignty and Schmitt's sovereign of the exception (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Britannica). It covers the theory that final lawmaking authority must rest in one place, not the later pluralist, internationalist or anarchist critics of it, nor the separate movements and doctrines that claim the word (sovereigntism, sovereign citizens, sovereign democracy, Hawaiian sovereignty, divine sovereignty in theology), which have their own entries.

keyFigures.role: Gave sovereignty its modern meaning: absolute, indivisible authority to declare the law
keyFigures.quote: The thinker who did the most to provide the term with its modern meaning was the English philosopher Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679)

keyFigures.role: Jurist who located sovereignty in the legislature as the source of positive law
keyFigures.quote: the English jurist John Austin (1790–1859) developed the concept further by investigating who exercises sovereignty in the name of the people or of the state

keyWorks.title: Leviathan
keyWorks.author: Thomas Hobbes
keyWorks.quote: Leviathan, which represented the abstract notion of the state

summary: Sovereignty is the doctrine that every political community has one supreme authority within its territory, with no higher human authority inside it or over it from outside. Bodin and Hobbes made it absolute and above human law; Rousseau placed it in the people and Austin in the legislature, and the sources disagree on who holds it. Its defining sources say little about policy, so most statements are unanswered.
